content: 1. A comprehensive dossier will be developed to substantiate the claim of disease elimination across the entire country. This dossier will be submitted to the World Health Organization (WHO) for verification. 2. Continuous monitoring of the leprosy situation at all sub-national levels will be conducted to ensure that these units achieve the designated cut-off levels required for the elimination of leprosy transmission. 3. Internal evaluations will be conducted by national teams using Leprosy Transmission Assessment Surveys (LTAS) when a second-tier sub-national unit reaches the cut-off level for transmission interruption. 4. Once internal evaluations of all sub-national units are completed, a dossier will be prepared, incorporating LTAS reports. This dossier will be submitted when the country claims to have achieved disease elimination. 5. An external evaluation team will be invited to verify the elimination of the disease at the national level. 6. National programs are encouraged to conduct basic and operational research to improve diagnostic capabilities, treatment regimens, and the identification of markers to assess leprosy transmission and elimination. One suggested indicator is the measurement of PGL-1 antibody levels in children within a defined community, which can also serve as a potential marker for assessing the magnitude of infection in the community. 7. The focus should remain on interrupting transmission and subsequently eliminating the disease, even if sporadic cases occur. This requires adherence to specific interventions and indicators outlined in the criteria for declaring transmission interruption. 8. Political commitment is essential, including the development of a National Strategic Plan for leprosy elimination, allocation of adequate resources, and alignment with global strategies such as the WHO Leprosy Strategy 2021–2030 and the NTD Roadmap 2021–2030. 9. Dedicated staff and capacity building for healthcare workers, including those in the private sector, are critical. Training programs, e-learning modules, and counseling services should be implemented to ensure the availability of trained staff at all levels. 10. Awareness programs targeting the general population, at-risk groups, school students, and workplaces should disseminate information on early symptoms and signs of leprosy to encourage health-seeking behavior. 11. Advocacy efforts should involve direct communication with politicians and bureaucrats through meetings, brochures, and written materials to emphasize the program's needs and sensitize decision-makers. 12. Partnerships with WHO, NGOs, philanthropists, and other relevant agencies should be established and sustained to secure adequate funding and accomplish specific tasks. 13. Early detection, diagnosis, and treatment of leprosy, including relapses, should be ensured through accessible services at the community level and designated referral centers. Flexible treatment models should be implemented to ensure treatment completion. 14. Continued care for individuals affected by primary and secondary disabilities, including mental health support, should be provided through skilled healthcare staff and appropriate infrastructure. 15. Effective surveillance and improved data management systems are necessary. This includes mapping patients, digitizing data, and utilizing web-based systems for planning and synchronizing drug supply management. 16. Contact tracing should involve listing and screening contacts of all new leprosy cases and cases detected in the past five years. Counseling should be provided to obtain consent for examinations, and annual screenings of neighbors and social contacts should be conducted for five years. 17. Post-exposure prophylaxis should be made available, including rifampicin and counseling services. Eligible contacts should receive single-dose rifampicin (SDR) chemoprophylaxis to maximize preventive chemotherapy coverage. 18. Documentation at the sub-national level and preparation of a country dossier are required when claiming leprosy elimination. The dossier should be submitted alongside a request for verification. 19. LTAS should be conducted to assess the epidemiological situation at sub-national levels, ensuring zero autochthonous cases for three consecutive years. Health facilities should align with referral system plans and standard operating procedures (SOPs). 20. Monitoring, evaluation, and verification mechanisms should be in place to assess cut-off levels, retrieve data annually, and compare trends for all indicators. WHO will verify the elimination claim through an international team. 21. In the post-elimination phase, national health plans should include surveillance for ten years in areas where elimination has been achieved. Surveillance should be conducted through sentinel or referral centers and apex health centers. 22. Dedicated staff and capacity building for healthcare workers should continue, with e-learning modules and integrated disability care provided at referral centers. Routine screening of contacts of confirmed leprosy cases should be maintained. 23. Advocacy with authorities should involve communication with politicians and bureaucrats to report sporadic cases and advocate for critical incident investigations.
